scenario: The generative track has 8 papers today, 5 with deep dives, and the common thread is making generative retrieval cheaper to serve. Pinterest's PinGER lets each history item cost one token at serving time. Taobao's SLIDE moves beam search offline so the model decodes greedily once online. ECNU's MuSID-KD aligns the student with the teacher at every SID level when distilling a small model. Tencent's LoopGR reuses one decoder in a loop instead of adding layers. Octen-WebGR scales generative retrieval to 200 million web pages and measures what it and dense retrieval are each good at. Teams putting generative retrieval into production can start with PinGER and SLIDE.

papers.title: PinGER: Token-Efficient Generative Retrieval with Semantic IDs
papers.authors: Xinyi Li, Sujan Reddy Ale, Yi-Ping Hsu, Zelun Wang, Yilin Chen, Hanyu Li, Hanlin Lu, Arkin Dharawat, Lulu Yao, Yaxin Li, Bella Huang, Xiangyi Chen, Jaewon Yang, Jiajing Xu, Charles Rosenberg
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval replaces nearest-neighbor search with token-by-token decoding of an item's semantic ID (SID). But existing SID-based methods primarily use L levels of tokens sequentially to represent each item in the input history. As a result, a fixed context window holds L times fewer items than it would with one embedding per item. We present PinGER, a generative retriever deployed at Pinterest that retains SID outputs while making input histories compact, built on three ideas. (1) An asymmetric attention mask over interleaved SID and dense tokens lets later items attend only to the dense ones, so the model is supervised at every SID position in training yet serves one token per item while computing the same function. (2) Generation is controllable through goal-conditioned outputs, reinforcement learning, and a prefix-diversity penalty, which together steer retrieval toward surface-specific goals and diverse candidates. (3) A serving stack built for efficient wide-beam generation is paired with decoding constrained to valid identifiers and candidate resolution from a host-local index. Deployed in Related Pins, PinGER lifts saves of fresh Pins by 3.60% and overall saves by 0.62%, while reducing the surface's end-to-end latency by 0.7% and eliminating the cost of the nearest-neighbor search it replaces.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval encodes each item as a multi-level SID and generates it level by level, but on the input side every history item costs several tokens. During training, Pinterest's PinGER places one dense-vector token after each item's SID and requires that any token reading another item may see only that item's dense token, never its SID. At serving time all SIDs in the history can be dropped, each item costs 1 token, and the output is unchanged. ==It turns input compression into a structural constraint at training time==. Offline it matches TIGER's 1,024-token recall with 170 tokens, and after launch on Related Pins saves rose 0.62%.

deep_reading.title: PinGER: Token-Efficient Generative Retrieval with Semantic IDs

papers.title: SLIDE: Search-to-List Item Distillation for Single-Rollout Generative Retrieval
papers.authors: Tianyu Zhan, Gui Ling, Ran Tao, Kunhai Lin, Tong Xiong, Wang Yang, Kaixuan Zhang, Zhihong Chen, Yuliang Yan, Dan Ou, Shengyu Zhang, Haihong Tang
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) typically relies on item-level beam search to retrieve candidates, leaving cross-item dependencies unmodeled and limiting direct optimization of list-level objectives. A natural alternative is to generate the entire list within a single autoregressive trajectory. However, greedy decoding with directly trained list-wise models substantially underperforms beam search. We identify two contributing factors: the broader search space explored by beam search and the positional bias of scarce positive signals, which deprives later positions of adequate supervision. To address these challenges, we propose $\textbf{SLIDE}$, a search-to-list item distillation framework that decouples offline search from online list generation. A teacher model retrieves high-quality candidates through offline item-level beam search, providing additional conversion-relevant supervision beyond sparse behavioral labels. Their Semantic IDs (SIDs) are then concatenated in beam-score order to form list-wise distillation targets. This search-to-list conversion transforms candidates retrieved along separate search paths into sequential item-generation targets within a single trajectory. Trained on these targets, the student generates the Top-$K$ list in a single greedy pass, also decoupling teacher scaling from online deployment. Experiments on FORGE and Taobao Search show that SLIDE substantially improves retrieval quality under single greedy decoding and, with stronger offline teachers, surpasses the beam-search reference. Supplementary RL experiments support the effectiveness of list-level generation.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval usually produces candidates online with beam search, and the beams never see each other; writing a whole list in one go by greedy decoding is the most direct alternative but works much worse. Taobao's SLIDE (a training method that distills offline search results into lists) moves search offline: a teacher runs beam search for every training request, concatenates the retrieved items in score order into one long sequence, and a student learns it, decoding greedily once online. ==It trades online search cost for offline labeling cost==. With a 7B teacher, the 0.5B student reaches HR@10 of 0.4578, beating the 0.4498 of beam search at the same size.

deep_reading.title: SLIDE: Search-to-List Item Distillation for Single-Rollout Generative Retrieval

papers.title: MuSID-KD: Multigranularity Knowledge Distillation for Generative Recommendation with Semantic IDs
papers.authors: Fengshi Zhang, Xiyan Ding, Shuxiao Xie, Wei Zhang
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation with semantic IDs (SIDs) represents each item as a sequence of discrete tokens and autoregressively predicts the next item's SID. Despite strong recommendation performance, repeated decoding over multiple SID positions incurs substantial inference cost. Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a powerful generative teacher to a lightweight student, yet conventional objectives do not fully account for multi-token SID generation. We identify two limitations: item-level distribution alignment may not adequately preserve the teacher's ranking of candidate groups sharing SID prefixes, while uniform alignment across SID positions may affect final item ranking differently. We propose MuSID-KD, which combines Hierarchical Candidate Distribution Alignment (HCDA) and Ranking Impact Guided Levelwise Distillation (RIGD). HCDA aggregates item probabilities according to shared SID prefixes and aligns candidate distributions at successive levels, from candidate groups to individual items. RIGD evaluates the reduction in pairwise ranking surrogate loss when one student score contribution is replaced with the teacher's contribution, and allocates supervision accordingly. Experiments on real-world recommendation datasets using three lightweight student architectures demonstrate improved recommendation accuracy and better alignment of prefix marginal distributions and pairwise item rankings, without modifying the student's online inference architecture. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/m7k2-review-83f9/.
papers.summary: When a SID-based generative recommender is distilled into a small model, the student is usually asked only to match the teacher's distribution over which item to recommend in the end. ECNU's MuSID-KD (a multi-granularity distillation method that works level by level over the SID) finds this is not enough: a student aligned only on items disagrees with the teacher on the order of candidate groups at intermediate SID levels in 53.8% of comparisons on average. ==The teacher's knowledge lives not only in the last-level item probabilities but also in the ranking of prefixes at every level==. On three Amazon datasets its NDCG@10 is 8.31% higher on average than basic distillation, with the online inference structure unchanged.

deep_reading.title: MuSID-KD: Multigranularity Knowledge Distillation for Generative Recommendation with Semantic IDs

papers.title: LoopGR: Parameter-Efficient Scaling for Generative Recommendation via Recurrent Depth
papers.authors: Huizhe Zhang, Yudong Li, Liang Chen, Chengxiang Zhuo, Zang Li
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation formulates item recommendation as autoregressive generation rather than a discriminative scoring problem. Although empirical studies exhibit favorable scaling behavior in recommendation, unleashing the benefits of scaling remains challenging under the strict model size and inference cost constraints of real-world systems. A central challenge is to combine expressive modeling of user-item interaction histories with flexible computational depth without proportionally increasing model size. We introduce LoopGR, a parameter-efficient scaling framework for generative recommendation via recurrent depth. LoopGR employs a tailored hierarchical recurrent depth mechanism that alternates between a shared generative decoder and a lightweight context updater. For efficient inference, we further develop recurrent trajectory self-distillation that distills a low-budget student from a high-budget teacher by aligning both predictive distributions and evolution directions. Extensive experiments show that LoopGR consistently outperforms strong generative recommendation baselines. Compared with a representative encoder-decoder baseline, LoopGR achieves superior performance while reducing model size by up to 52%. These results establish recurrent depth as a new scaling dimension, offering a flexible and resource-efficient scaling path for generative recommendation.
papers.summary: Making a generative recommender stronger usually means adding layers, which means adding parameters and memory. Tencent's LoopGR (a generative recommendation backbone that reuses one decoder in a loop) runs the same decoder several times. Between passes, the decoder's BOS hidden state (its current judgement of the target) is added to every history position and a tiny GRU rewrites the history along the item order. ==The decoder keeps revising its prediction, and the history changes along with it==. At equal compute it beats an encoder-decoder backbone with about half the parameters; on industrial data its Recall@10 is 0.6458, above the production model BARGE's 0.6277.

deep_reading.title: LoopGR: Parameter-Efficient Scaling for Generative Recommendation via Recurrent Depth

papers.title: DPE-Rec: Diversity-Preserving and Efficient Diffusion Language Model Recommendation for Bundle Construction
papers.authors: Pingchuan Ma, Bohan Jiang, Chengshuai Zhao, Dawei Li, Zhen Tan, Huan Liu
papers.abstract: Generative bundle construction completes a partially observed bundle by generating its missing items from a large product catalog. Compared to autoregressive LLMs, diffusion LLM emerges as a natural fit for this unordered generation task. Their bidirectional attention provides an inductive bias better aligned with unordered bundle construction. Iterative denoising can reveal multiple tokens per step, potentially reducing inference latency. However, directly applying DLMs to this task presents two key challenges: 1 Despite its flexible reveal order, confidence-guided decoding tends to postpone semantic-fork decisions until refinement tokens constrain their choices, reducing bundle diversity. 2 Revealing more tokens per step can compromise recommendation quality, stifling the potential for faster inference. We introduce DPE-Rec, a diffusion framework for diversity preservation and efficient recommendation. DPE-Rec preserves diversity by introducing semantic-fork-aware GRPO, which prioritizes semantic-fork decisions via autoregressive rollouts. It improves efficiency through pseudo-trajectory distillation, which concentrates learning from the vast random corruption space onto the compact trajectory-induced subspace visited by high-quality decoding, unlocking reliable multi-token decoding. Together, these components enable diverse and accurate bundle construction with substantially fewer denoise steps. Experiments on multiple bundle construction benchmarks show that DPE-Rec improves recommendation performance by 63% on average, and its fast variant achieves 25.6$times$ faster inference on average than existing generative recommendation arts, with minimal loss in recommendation quality.
papers.summary: Completing a product bundle or playlist is unordered generation of a set of items, so a diffusion language model with bidirectional attention suits it, and it can reveal several tokens per step. Each item is a multi-level SID whose first token decides the coarse category, but with confidence-ordered revealing the model postpones that token, so generated items look alike; revealing too many at once assembles SIDs that do not exist. DPE-Rec (a diffusion recommendation framework for bundle construction) generates the category token first during reinforcement-learning rollouts with a higher sampling temperature at that token, and trains denoising not on random masks but only on the intermediate states that slow one-token-per-step decoding actually visits. ==Decide which way to branch first, then fill in the details==. On set-matching metrics such as F1, it beats existing generative recommenders by 63% on average.

papers.title: Octen-WebGR: Scaling Generative Retrieval to 200 Million Web Pages
papers.authors: Guangwei Xu, Wenkai Zhang, Yawen Liu, Dongxu Zhang, Xijie Xu, Kuan Zou
papers.abstract: Navigational search aims to find a single target page among hundreds of millions of web pages. Click tables work well for queries seen before but cannot generalise to new formulations, while embedding retrievers generalise across content but often rank navigational targets poorly. We introduce Octen-WebGR, a generative retrieval framework that stores web pages in the parameters of a language model: given a query, the model generates a two-token semantic identifier constrained to a table of real URLs. We develop Octen-WebGR-4B, which indexes 201 million web pages, and evaluate it on real navigational traffic from the month after training. Generative retrieval is most effective on new ways of asking for familiar pages: for unseen queries targeting pages with substantial interaction history, it ranks the correct page first 30.9% of the time, against 17.2% for a dense retriever trained on the same clicks (21.4% with a click prior). Embedding retrieval keeps an advantage on rarely visited pages, so the two approaches generalise on complementary sides, the query and the page. Over all navigational traffic, Octen-WebGR reaches 59.6% top-1 accuracy, against 46.5% for a click-enhanced dense retriever and up to 37.5% for frontier LLMs answering from memory, which cost at least 40 times as much per query. The 4B model runs on a single GPU with 10 GB of memory, compared with 412 GB for exact dense retrieval. Scaling experiments with up to 32 million URLs show that, when every query-page pair is seen equally often, the model size needed grows sublinearly with index size, and that retrieval is constrained more by page exposure than by model capacity. We release Octen-WebGR-4B and Octen-WebGR-0.6B with their identifier tables and inference code.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval has stayed below ten million documents. The Octen team's Octen-WebGR (a model that does web navigational search with generative retrieval) pushes it to 201 million web pages: every page is named by two tokens, a 4B model generates them directly from the query, and a table lookup returns the URL. On real navigational traffic from the month after training, it ranks the target first 59.6% of the time, against 46.5% for a dense retriever trained on the same clicks and reranked by clicks. ==Writing click history into the weights teaches the model how popular each page is==, so it can pick the page users want among several similar pages of the same site. On rarely clicked pages dense retrieval is still better, so the two are complementary.

deep_reading.title: Octen-WebGR: Scaling Generative Retrieval to 200 Million Web Pages

papers.title: ReflectRec: Cycle-Consistency Preference Verification for LLM-based Recommendation
papers.authors: Dae Kyoo Kim, Heejung Cho, Sungmoo Hong, Eunil Park
papers.abstract: CoT-style LLM recommenders generate a natural-language preference note as a chain-of-thought prefix to ranking, but the note is trusted without verification, and the ranker never consults behaviorally similar users. We propose ReflectRec, organized around a preference-to-history round-trip verifier whose recall score serves as an operational signal of preference-to-history recoverability, enabling conditional regeneration for low-recoverability preferences and selection among regeneration attempts. Around this verifier, we wire a semantic Stage-1 prompt, conditional regeneration, and Forward-Look retrieval that injects future watches of behaviorally similar users as a collaborative hint. On MovieLens-100K and MovieLens-1M, the full pipeline outperforms CoT4Rec-ICL by +16.25 / +4.46 pp Hit@10, with positive gains across all ValScore buckets and three LLM backbones (Qwen3-30B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Llama-3.3-70B).
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought LLM recommenders first write a user preference note and then rank, but the note is never checked and the ranker never consults behaviorally similar users. ReflectRec (an LLM recommendation method that verifies preference notes by a round trip) has the model guess which movies the user watched from the note alone, and uses the share of the real history it recovers as the note's trust score. Low-scoring notes are regenerated and the highest-scoring attempt is kept, while movies that similar users watched next are injected into the prompt as a collaborative hint. ==Whether a preference description can recover the history is the test of whether it can be trusted==. On MovieLens-1M, Hit@10 is 4.46 points above the CoT4Rec baseline.

papers.title: Transporting Quantiles to Codebook: Scalable Vector Quantization without Codebook Collapse
papers.abstract: Effective discrete representation learning with VQ-VAE serves as a fundamental component of modern autoregressive generative models. However, it is widely known to suffer from codebook collapse and inefficient code utilization. To address this issue, we propose FlowVQ, a simple yet effective alternative to standard vector quantization by formulating neural quantization as a joint modeling and clustering process. Specifically, we learn the latent space using a lightweight flow matching model alongside training, corresponding to a probability flow ODE that transports an often fixed well-behaved source distribution while preserving probability mass. Based on this, we define the codebook C_1 by transporting even-quantile partitioned prior codes C_0 from the source space through the learned flow, and obtaining the Voronoi centroids under the induced distribution, leading to a structured discretization. We evaluated on image tokenization and generation, as well as on two tasks requiring high-precision tokenization, demonstrating scalability and improved expressivity of the codebook with full utilization.
papers.summary: Vector quantization underlies image and audio generation and even recommendation SIDs, but the common VQ-VAE codebook often collapses, leaving most codewords unused. FlowVQ (a flow-matching-based vector quantization method) first cuts a fixed simple prior distribution into cells of equal probability, one initial codeword per cell. A lightweight flow model trained together with the VQ-VAE then maps the prior space one-to-one onto the data's latent space. The map preserves probability mass, so each cell still holds the same share of the data after transport, and the codewords are the centers of the transported cells. ==Even code usage becomes a property of the map itself==. On material structure reconstruction it reaches a 90.81% match rate with the whole codebook in use.
